synergies.why: Six cards in the pool gate on the SAME board state — a battlefield holding exactly one other unit you control, or exactly two units there — and Disciple of Shen is the one that pays for itself: standing beside any single one of the other five satisfies BOTH cards' count at once, since each one is the other's "one other unit". 383.2.a.1 makes the count part of the Trigger Condition for the two Hold payoffs (Shen, Leader of the Kinkou Order's point, Shen, Scourge of Shadows' draw), so it is checked when the trigger is placed, not when it resolves; Sacred Protector's combat-damage gate and Hand Hammer's Might Bonus are continuous, read whenever asked; and Keeper of Law's discount and Shadow Dash's +1 Might both read the board at the moment they are used. 185.2.d — "Tokens have a type. They follow all rules for their type unless otherwise specified" — is the trap the list cannot show: a token from any faucet in the deck is a third unit at that battlefield, and every one of these six conditions breaks at once.

synergies.name: Unyielding Spirit's fog leaves the whole "deal damage equal to Might" removal suite standing
synergies.why: 417.6.b.3 names Challenge as its own worked example: "The damage that Challenge causes to be dealt is dealt by the chosen units, not by Challenge" — so the ten cards that deal damage equal to a unit's Might (Challenge, Carnivorous Snapvine, Dragon's Rage, Gentlemen's Duel, Marching Orders, Rampage, Clash of Giants, Strike Down, Alpha Strike, Last Breath) are all UNIT damage, never spell or ability damage. Unyielding Spirit's "Prevent all spell and ability damage this turn" (437.4: "not considered to have been dealt to it at all") therefore blanks every burn spell in the format while leaving this whole removal family untouched — a deck can run both the fog and the kill suite with no tension between them.

synergies.name: Syndra, Transcendent grants a SECOND, independent [Repeat] instance to a spell that already prints one

excludes.why: Curtain Call carries no [Action] or [Reaction]; 155 confines a plain spell to an Open State outside Showdowns, so it can never be played while Syndra is in a showdown.
Desert's Call carries no [Action] or [Reaction], the same 155 gate.
Double Trouble carries no [Action] or [Reaction], the same 155 gate.
Piercing Light carries no [Action] or [Reaction], the same 155 gate.
Rocket Barrage carries no [Action] or [Reaction], the same 155 gate.
Square Up carries no [Action] or [Reaction], the same 155 gate.
Temptation carries no [Action] or [Reaction], the same 155 gate.
Upstage Comedy carries no [Action] or [Reaction], the same 155 gate.

synergies.why: "While I'm in a showdown, your spells have [Repeat] 2 Energy + 1 Chaos" is a grant, and 820.1.c.2 keeps a granted instance independent of a printed one: "If a spell or ability has more than one instance of Repeat, each Cost may be paid or not paid individually." A spell with no printed Repeat gets one bonus execution from her; a spell that already prints [Repeat] (Existential Dread, Hard Bargain, Frigid Touch, Danger Zone, and the rest of the twelve left after the exclusions) can pay BOTH costs for three total executions off one card, which is why the printed-Repeat spells are the interesting partner and not merely any spell. 155 with 806.1.b / 813.1.b is the gate that removes eight of the twenty candidate spells outright: none of them carries the permission to be played inside the Showdown her static requires. Re-audited 2026-09-09 for the routes into a showdown that are NOT the two printed keywords: none of the eight excluded spells carries [Hidden] (811.1.b's tail is what hands a face-down card [Reaction] from the following turn), and no card in the pool grants [Reaction] to a spell — swept, the only two grants of the keyword are SFD-054 Jax, Unmatched (to your Equipment, via [Quick-Draw]) and VEN-160 Mystic Vortex (which only taxes cards that already have it). All twelve partners were re-read and every one prints [Action] or [Reaction]. SFD-122 Called Shot is banned in both formats and SFD-182 Danger Zone is Fury/Mind against a mono-Chaos anchor; neither is an exclude, because `playableUnder` drops a banned or out-of-identity card at match time and the authored list is the pool, not one shell.

synergies.name: Gearhead doubles the printed Might Bonus of any Equipment attached to him
synergies.why: "Each Equipment attached to me gives double its base Might bonus" reads the PRINTED number: 137.3 defines a Might Bonus as a modulation applied while Attached, 477.3.d applies it in the Might-Bonus layer, and 718.4 ties it to "the value listed" on the card — so Gearhead's own text is unambiguous about which number it is doubling. Thirty-four Equipment in the pool carry a positive Might Bonus, from Long Sword's +1 to Trinity Force's larger printed value, and every one of them is worth twice as much attached to him as to any other body, with no extra cost beyond the [Equip].

synergies.name: Kinkou Temple pays every [Tank] unit standing there, doubling the wall it already was
synergies.why: "Units here with [Tank] have +1 Might" reads any Tank source, printed or granted, and 815.1.c.2 is what makes a Tank body's Might a price rather than decoration: "Units without Tank are invalid assignments until all units with Tank have lethal damage assigned to them." A wall is priced in the damage needed to clear it (465.2.c.4 caps assignment at minimum lethal), so +1 Might on a Tank body does not add a point of stat, it adds a point the ATTACKER must spend before touching anything else there — and since the bill scales with every Tank body present, the battlefield doubles the cost of a multi-body wall (four 1-Might Tank tokens cost 4 elsewhere; at the Temple, at 2 Might each, the bill is 8). Twenty-five cards in the pool print [Tank], from a single 1-Might token grantor (Lillia, Protector of Dreams' "Your token units have [Tank]") to a legend's own repeating grant (Eye of Twilight).

synergies.name: Eye of Twilight's [Action] Tank grant lands on a [Shield] body, whose defending Might is the threshold nothing can clear
synergies.why: 815.1.c.2 is the load-bearing sentence: "Units without Tank are invalid assignments until all units with Tank have lethal damage assigned to them." So an attack whose summed Might cannot reach the Tank's CURRENT Might assigns nothing anywhere, and the whole garrison survives — the Tank's own Might is the only lever, because 815.2 makes a second Tank grant redundant. 814.1.c makes [Shield] "While I am a defender, I have +X [M]" and 814.1.d.1 keeps it in effect as long as the Defender designation lasts, so a [Shield] body's threshold is exactly the number that matters and exists only at the moment it matters; 814.2 sums a second granted instance on top. The legend's ability is [Action], and 806.1.c.2 lets it be activated during showdowns on any player's turn, so the grant is bought AFTER 464.2.c.3 has designated the attackers and their summed Might is countable. It must NOT go on the [Backline] body: 465.2.c.8 names Caitlyn, Patrolling by name as the worked example of an exclusionary pair and hands the choice back to the attacker. This rule REPLACES `eye-of-twilight-protects-backline`, refuted 2026-09-09: 465.2.c.6 already puts a Backline body last, so granting Tank to some OTHER body left its position unchanged and the Backline card was a bystander rather than a partner.

synergies.name: Counter Strike is the one save that never relocates what it protects, so a "while I'm at a battlefield" clause survives it
synergies.why: 455 makes a Recall a relocation to the BASE, so a heal-exhaust-recall shield (Guardian Angel, Zhonya's Hourglass) switches off any "While I'm at a battlefield" clause for the whole turn it saves the body. Counter Strike is different: 437.4 — "prevent it" — means the damage is never dealt at all, so the unit never dies, never gets recalled, and never leaves; 437.5 lets it apply inside the damage step itself, at [Reaction] speed. Fourteen units in the pool carry a printed "While I'm at a battlefield" clause, from a static (Mageseeker Warden's lockdown, Tianna Crownguard's point denial, Sandstone Chimera's rune tax) to an ability restriction (Renata Glasc, Mastermind's and Xerath, Freed's own text: "Use this ability only while I'm at a battlefield") — Counter Strike is the one save in the pool that keeps every one of them switched on.

synergies.name: Heedless Resurrection's "ignoring its cost" only zeroes the BASE cost, so a reanimated [Accelerate] body can still pay to enter ready
synergies.why: 356.1.b.1 sets only the base Energy and Power cost to zero, and 356.1.b.3 spells out the rest with Legion Rearguard as its own worked example: "They ignore Legion Rearguard's Base Cost of 2 Energy, but the optional additional cost of 1 Energy and 1 Fury Power is added to its Total Cost and must be paid." Heedless Resurrection plays a body from the trash "ignoring its cost" for no more Energy or Power than the unit it killed to pay for it — but 143.4.a ("This can be altered by Accelerate or similar game effects") is a separate, optional cost the reanimated body can still choose to pay, entering ready instead of exhausted. Twenty-six units in the pool print [Accelerate], so the free half of the spell (the reanimation) and the paid half (the readying) are two different costs on the same card, and the second one is never waived by the first.

synergies.name: Allay's granted [Deflect] sums with any second source standing at her battlefield

excludes.why: Decree of Insight IGNORES [Deflect] while paying its own cost; it never grants the keyword to anything, so it adds nothing to a stack and is the opposite of a partner.
Heisho, Shell of the World lets BOTH players ignore [Deflect] there, which works against Allay's whole point rather than adding to it.

Spirit's Refuge grants "[Deflect] if they didn't already". Every other friendly unit at Allay's battlefield already has it, so the grant is placed on nothing and 809.2 has no second instance to sum — the second-trigger-is-a-no-op shape, scoped to this rule (away from Allay the same card is a fine Deflect source). Swept 2026-09-09: it is the only conditional grant in the pool (`grep -inE "if they didn'?t already"` returns one row).

synergies.why: 809.2 sums granted Deflect exactly as 807.2 sums granted Assault and 814.2 sums granted Shield: "the Deflect Value of all granted Deflect keywords is summed." "While I'm at a battlefield, your other units here have [Deflect]" is Allay's free, permanent instance, so a body that already prints [Deflect] (Fiora, Victorious while Mighty; Jhin, Murderous Artist; Rengar, Unseen) or already carries a numbered grant (Jayce, Hammer in Hand's [Deflect 2]) costs the opponent MORE rainbow to interact with at her battlefield than either source manages alone — 809.3 makes the resulting Deflect value "a characteristic of the permanent" that a card like Master Yi, Tempered's own [Level 6] grant can check and stack on top of.

synergies.name: Wielder of Water pays itself the same "alone" toll it charges its two partners
synergies.why: 740.2.a — "A unit is alone when there are no other friendly units at the same location" — is an own-side measurement (the pool's own reminder text on Lonely Poro says the same), so the enemy garrison never breaks the condition. Wielder of Water's own "+2 Might while attacking or defending alone" already qualifies whenever it stands by itself, and it needs no partner to pay for; the pairing this rule names is the deckbuilding fact that Mask of Foresight ("give it +1 Might this turn") and Wuju Bladesman - Starter ("+2 Might") key on the identical own-side condition, so a deck that keeps a single body at each battlefield turns all three on simultaneously with no card doing double duty. `SFD-036 Lonely Poro`'s [Deathknell] ("If I died alone, draw 1") and its printed inverse `UNL-156 Loyal Poro` ("If I didn't die alone, draw 1") key on the same state read at a different moment — a thin board that keeps this rule's three cards live also keeps Lonely Poro's Deathknell paying and switches Loyal Poro's off.

synergies.name: Hidden Blade's second sentence survives a save, so aim it at your own shielded body and draw 2

excludes.why: "If it would die this turn, banish it instead" is a replacement that still REMOVES the unit — and 808.1.d.1's example is exactly this shape, so it also erases the Deathknell. It is the one member of the family that cannot keep a body on the board.

synergies.why: Hidden Blade reads "Kill a unit at a battlefield. Its controller draws 2." 359.3.e.14.b: "If the Game Action performed in an earlier linked instruction is replaced, this will not affect the later linked instruction, unless the later linked instruction directly references the Game Action being performed." The draw references "its controller", i.e. the unit, never the kill — so a would-die replacement on YOUR OWN body keeps the body and still pays the two cards, for E2 + 1 Power, or for nothing at all from face down. The trap is the sibling paragraph, 359.3.e.14.a: "If the earlier linked instruction is ignored for any reason, the later linked instruction will also be ignored" — so a target that has merely LEFT the battlefield (bounced, recalled) makes the whole card fizzle, while a target that is genuinely saved by a replacement does not. Every survivor in this list replaces the death rather than dodging it: 808.1.d.1 names the heal / exhaust / recall shape by name, and 455 sends the saved body to its base, which is a cost for anything with "While I'm at a battlefield" on it. Altar of Blood is the one conditional member — it replaces a death "during combat" only, so the Blade has to be played inside the showdown (it is [Action]) rather than in the Main Phase.

synergies.name: The Warden herds the enemy into their base, where only removal with no location clause can follow

partner.textMatches: (?:[Kk]ill|[Bb]anish) (?:a|an|one|all|up to one)(?: enemy)? units?[.,]|[Dd]eal \d+ to (?:a|an|one|all) units?[.,]

excludes.why: "Banish a unit, then its owner plays it to the same location, ignoring its cost" gives the unit straight back — it is a blink, not removal, so it takes nothing off the board the Warden has filled.

synergies.why: "While I'm at a battlefield, opponents can only play units to their base", and 054.2 — "If a card specifies that an action can 'only' be performed under certain circumstances, it cannot be performed under any other circumstances" — makes that a prohibition that beats 355.2.a's default and the seven cards that grant a wider play location. The consequence nobody prices is that the enemy board becomes a BASE, and almost every removal card in the pool prints "at a battlefield" or "here" and cannot see it. The list is every card whose target clause ends at the word "unit" with no location at all, which is what makes it reach a base: Vengeance is the only single-target kill with neither a location clause nor any other gate, The Ruination is the sweeper, Harnessed Dragon is a play trigger that kills anywhere, and the six damage rows (Falling Star, Icathian Rain, Super Mega Death Rocket!, Final Spark, Dancing Grenade, Xerath, Freed) reach a base as surely as a clause that says so. Two members the predicate cannot see and a reader should know about: VEN-131 Decree of Unity has no location clause either but its sentence continues "unit or gear", and the three cards that NAME a unit "in a base" (Rocket Barrage, Yone Blademaster, Curtain Call) say it in words the regex is not looking for. The Warden's second sentence — spells and abilities can't ready enemy units and gear — is a separate lock and is not what this rule is about.

synergies.name: A Fury cost written at the start of a trigger is paid to FINALIZE it, and a 0-Energy Seal is the only Power banked in time
synergies.why: 204.3.a: "When Costs within Instructions appear as the first part of the effect in triggered abilities, the cost is taken to be the base cost of the triggered ability. It must be paid to finalize the triggered ability." 312.2.c then shuts the door on finding the Power afterwards — "When the turn is in a Closed State, all pending chain items finish being finalized" — so nobody receives priority between the trigger firing and the cost being due. Every card in this list is therefore priced wrong if it is read as pay-on-resolution: the Fury Power has to already be in the pool when the discard happens, when the spell kills, when the attack is declared, or when the shielded body would die. Seal of Rage is E0 for 1 Fury Power and its ability is [Reaction], so it costs no slot in the turn's Energy and it is ready again every Awakening under 415.3.a — which matters because a rune tapped on your own turn pays nothing but Power on the opponent's (164.2.a costs the rune's exhaust, 164.2.b does not), and three of these triggers fire on a turn that is not yours. Draven, Vanquisher is banned in both formats (data/legality.json) and is listed only because the predicate reads card text; Seal of Insight is the identical answer in Mind, where Ava Achiever is the whole family.

synergies.name: Winning a combat means being the only side left, so an [Action] kill inside the showdown is what fires these five
synergies.why: 466.3.a: "A Player has won a combat if they received either the attacker or defender designation and are the only Player that has units remaining at this battlefield during this step." That is stricter than the reminder text these cards print (Nidalee says "I win if I remain after combat"), and 466.3.d makes it "No Result" if BOTH players still have units — with 466.1.a.2 recalling your attackers whenever defenders remain, and 466.1.a.1's "Heal all Units" wiping the marks that would have finished them. So a defence that merely survives pays nothing, and a trade pays nothing. Drag Under is [Action], costs E2 less from anywhere other than your hand, and kills a unit at a battlefield — played inside the combat the attack opened, after 464.2.c.3 has handed out the designations, it empties the defender's side and turns a No Result into a win with no damage step at all (465.1 needs both sides present for the damage tasks). Draven, Vanquisher is banned in both formats and is listed only because the predicate reads card text.

synergies.name: Bonus Damage is paid per Deal ACTION, so the Tome is worth what the spell's own repetitions are worth

excludes.why: "Choose a friendly unit. It deals damage equal to its Might split among enemy units" — 417.6.b.3 makes that UNIT damage, not the spell's, so the Tome (which pumps a spell) never reaches it. Volibear, Furious is absent from this list for the same reason under types: an ability is not a spell.

synergies.why: "[exhaust]: The next spell you play this turn deals 1 Bonus Damage", and 713 makes Bonus Damage "an intrinsic property that can be granted to Deal actions". 715.2 is the paragraph that prices it: "If the Deal action has multiple targets, the amount of Damage dealt to each target is increased by Bonus Damage individually and separately." So the Tome pays per Deal ACTION and, inside one action, per TARGET — never per point of damage. Both halves are in this list. Falling Star prints "Deal 3 to a unit" twice and collects two; Icathian Rain prints it six times and collects six; Piercing Light's "then deal 2 to up to one other unit" is a second action; and Unchecked Power is the multi-target case, where one Deal reaches every unit at battlefields and each of them takes the extra point separately. A single big spell collects once, which is why the pool's 8-damage Final Spark is not here. What the Tome never does is double: 714 sums every instance of Bonus Damage and applies it once, so a second source (Annie, Fiery, Void Gate, Rabadon's Deathcrown) is +1 more per action, not x2, and 715.4 keeps Bonus Damage from creating a Deal action of its own. Two families are deliberately outside the list. The three cards that print "deal N to it INSTEAD" — Sudden Storm, Monster Harpoon, Ruthless Strike — are one Deal action with a replaced amount, so they collect once. And the split cases (715.3: "If the Deal action Splits damage, then the Bonus Damage applies to the amount of Damage that will be Split. This can alter the number of targets eligible to be chosen") belong to Annie rather than to the Tome: Volibear's split is an ABILITY and Alpha Strike's is dealt by a chosen unit under 417.6.b.3, and the Tome pumps a spell.

synergies.name: Breakneck Mech is what lets a base-born Mech token cross the board at all
synergies.why: "Your Mechs have [Deflect] and [Ganking]", and 187.4 — "A 3 [M] Mech token is a domainless unit token with 3 Might and the Mech tag" — gives every Mech TOKEN that tag by rule, so the static reaches bodies no decklist can show. The reason it is worth a slot rather than a keyword is 144.4: the Standard Move goes only base to battlefield (144.4.a) and battlefield to base (144.4.b), and 144.4.c.1 is the single exception, "Units with Ganking may use their Standard Move to Move from Battlefield to Battlefield." A Mech born at your base is otherwise committed to one battlefield for the rest of its life, which is the bottleneck under every token line in this project; the Deflect half prices the opponent's answer at one rainbow per choice (809.1.c) on a board of bodies that cost you nothing. 810.1.c.3 is the limit to state with it — Ganking "does not give additional abilities or activations of Movement, only new options for the Standard Move" — so this is a wider destination, never a second move, and 810.2 makes a second grant redundant. The list is the Mech tag and nothing else: Mega-Mech has no rules text at all, and Experimental Hexplate cannot appear because it is an Equipment that says "I am a Mech" rather than carrying the tag.

synergies.name: A Gold token is a GEAR, so every Gold producer in the list is also a gear count
synergies.why: "When you play me, if you control 3 or more other gear, draw 1." 187.5 defines the token — "A Gold gear token is a domainless gear token with '[Reaction][>] Kill this, [E]: [Add] [A]'" — and 185.2.d makes it count: "Tokens have a type. They follow all rules for their type unless otherwise specified." So a Gold on your board is a gear for every gear-count threshold in the pool, it costs no card and no deck slot, and 103.2.b does not cap it. The catch is the token's own [E] in its cost: a Gold minted on a Hold or a Conquer enters exhausted and cannot pay for itself until your next Awakening (415.3.a), unless Renata Glasc, Industrialist is out — which is exactly why hoarding Golds rather than cashing them is what feeds a count. Card Sharp is in the list and is the one member that also hands the opponent a Gold (182 lets a spell name a different player as a token's controller), so it advances their gear count too.

synergies.name: The one XP payoff that reads a TURN instead of a threshold, so spending never switches it off
synergies.why: "If you've gained XP this turn, I have +1 Might and [Ganking]." Every other XP payoff in the pool is a [Level N] rung, and 824.1.d makes those fragile — "The Dependent Ability will be Inactive as soon as the controlling player has less than [N] XP" — while 730.2 says spending is your own reduction: "To Spend XP, reduce the value of XP marked on the Player spending it." So a list that runs an XP SINK turns its own [Level] rungs off, and the Newtfish is the single card that does not care, because the event it reads is the gain and not the balance. That makes every faucet in this list live for it, including the ones a Level deck cannot afford to pair with a sink, and it makes the Newtfish the correct payoff in a deck built to spend. 823.1.c.1 is why [Hunt] is in the predicate — "When I Conquer or Hold, my controller gains X XP" — and 315.2.b.2 holds every battlefield you control, so [Hunt] pays twice a turn on a Duel table (485.4). Gemhand Hunter is the card that carries one clause of each kind, so in a spending list its Hunt half keeps paying while its Level half goes dark.

synergies.name: Cull the Weak is a 2-Energy sacrifice outlet that no [Deflect] and no "can't be chosen" can answer
synergies.why: "Each player kills one of their units" is 355.10.e's own printed worked example: "It is part of a set of objects chosen in whole or in part by other players. e.g., 'Each player kills a unit they control' does not target. Each player, including the one who played the spell, chooses a unit to kill as the spell or ability resolves." Nothing is targeted and nothing is chosen by you on their side, so 809.1.c's [Deflect] tax — "an amount of Power equal to [Deflect Value] more to play as an additional cost for each time they choose" — is never charged, and an absolute "I can't be chosen by enemy spells and abilities" body is not consulted either. What that buys is a sacrifice outlet for two Energy and one Power that is also a piece of removal, and this list is what pays for your half: every Deathknell body and every card that watches a friendly unit die. Two limits to state rather than hide. The opponent picks their own casualty, so the removal half takes their worst body and is never an answer to a particular threat. And the payoff you kill has to be a body you can spare — 428.1.a.1.b snapshots a dying unit's location and attributes before the kill instruction completes, which is what makes Loyal Poro's "if I didn't die alone" reliably true when other friendlies stand with it.

synergies.name: A [Repeat] cost is SPENT in full, so a cheap spell crosses a threshold a discounted expensive one fails
synergies.why: "If you've spent 4 Energy or more to play a spell this turn, I have +4 Might." The whole lens splits on one word: a "costs N or more" clause reads the PRINTED cost under 206 and a discount never touches it, while a "spent N or more" clause reads what actually left the Rune Pool (166.2, 203.1, 356.4.b) and a discount switches it off. The constructive half is this list. 820.1.c.1 makes a [Repeat] cost "an Additional Cost to be paid during the steps of playing the spell or ability" — so it is SPENT, in full, on top of the base cost — while 206's second worked example (Defy against Rocket Barrage) says a "costs N" check ignores it entirely. So a 2-Energy spell with a 2-Energy Repeat spends 4 and arms the Neophyte, where a 6-Energy spell discounted to 3 does not. Read each spell's own Repeat cost before counting it: several in this list price the repeat in Power alone, which spends no Energy and clears nothing here. The same arithmetic works from the other side, and it is the one place an opponent helps you — 809.1.c makes [Deflect] an additional cost too, so their tax on your spell pushes you over your own line.

synergies.name: Purifier turns every Equipment on a body into a separate [Assault] instance, and 807.2 sums them
synergies.why: "Your Equipment each give [Assault]" — the word is EACH, so a body wearing three Equipment is granted three instances, and 807.2 collects them: "If a Unit has Assault or has been granted Assault and is granted Assault by an additional source, the Assault Value of all granted Assault keywords is summed", with Riot's example (Petty Officer plus Cleave reaching Assault 4) doing the arithmetic. 807.1.b.3 makes a bare grant worth 1, so the sum is simply the number of Equipment, on top of every Might Bonus those Equipment already add under 137.3 and 434.1.d. Two limits worth carrying. 807.1.c is conditional — "While I am an attacker, I have +X [M]" — and 807.1.d makes being an attacker mean the Unit gained the Attacker designation during Combat, so none of it exists on a bloodless conquer where 323.9 stages no Combat at all. And stacking Equipment on one carrier is its own problem: 818.1 makes each [Equip] a separate Activated Ability with its own cost, [Weaponmaster] frees only one and only "to me", and 434.1.g means re-attaching to the current host does nothing.

synergies.name: "Kill all DAMAGED enemy units" reads a marker, not a threshold — so any ping in the list is universal removal
synergies.why: 143.2.a is death BY damage — "If a Unit ever has nonzero damage marked on it equalling or exceeding its Might, it is Killed" — but Warwick's sweep is a kill BY EFFECT keyed on the word "damaged", so it ignores Might entirely and two points off a 3-Energy gear kill a 10-Might body as dead as a 1-Might one. Every card in this list marks damage cheaply and repeatedly, which is the only input the sweep needs. The clock is 466.1.a.1 — the Combat Cleanup inserts "3c. Heal all Units" — so a mark applied in a previous combat, or on the opponent's turn, is gone before your attack: the ping and the attack are the same Main Phase. For the play-trigger and exhaust members that is simply an ordering; for the members whose ping is itself an attack trigger the interaction is finer, and this project has walked it — 383.3.d lets the controller order simultaneous triggers, 340.1 resolves the newest finalized item first, so a ping trigger PLACED second resolves FIRST and marks damage that Warwick's kill trigger then reads on execution under 359.3.f.2. Warwick's own clause carries no extra condition, so 383.2.a.1 has nothing to freeze at the designation.

synergies.name: 428.5.c is the only reason a damage spell ever counts as killing with a spell

excludes.why: "Deal 3 to a unit at a battlefield. If it would die this turn, banish it instead" replaces the death, so no kill action is ever generated and 428.5.c has nothing to attribute — the one damage spell in the pool that provably cannot fire this trigger.

synergies.why: "When you kill a unit with a spell, you may pay 1 Energy + 1 Fury to play me from your trash." No burn spell in the pool contains a kill instruction, and 143.2.a kills in a Cleanup rather than on resolution, so without one paragraph this trigger would never fire off damage at all. 428.5.c is that paragraph: "When one or more Units is killed due to a Cleanup, that kill action is attributed to the spell or ability that resolved immediately prior to that Cleanup that dealt damage to the Unit or Units", with 428.5.c.1 making the player responsible for the deal action responsible for the kill. 428.5.c.2 is the exception that keeps the trigger honest in combat — a kill in the COMBAT Cleanup is attributed to the units that dealt the damage, not to any spell — so a body that simply dies fighting pays nothing. Read with 428.5.d, a spell that splits itself into a reflexive ability keeps the attribution, since "Abilities originating from Game Objects that are attributed Kill Actions are attributed in addition to the Game Object that created them". The cost sits at the start of the trigger's effect, so 204.3.a makes it a base cost paid to FINALIZE: bank the Fury Power before you cast, because 312.2.c gives you no window afterwards.

synergies.name: Atakhan's additional cost reads the PRINTED cost of the body you feed it, both halves of it
synergies.why: "You may kill a friendly unit as an additional cost to play me. If you do, I cost 1 Energy less for each Energy it costs and 1 Order Power less for each Power it costs." 206 fixes which number that is — the PRINTED cost, whatever was actually paid — so a body played at a discount, from [Hidden] for zero, or reanimated for free still pays Atakhan its full printed value, and this list is every unit in the pool printed at 8 Energy or more. At E10 + 3 Order Power he is the most expensive body most lists can field; one 8-Energy corpse takes him to E2, and 356.6 floors each half at 0 rather than letting either go negative. Two things a reader should know before building it. The cheapest fuel of all is not in this list and cannot be: 185.3.a.1 makes an ordinary token's cost "0 for all purposes", but 185.3.a.2 appends a real cost to a Reflection through the copy effect, so a LeBlanc Reflection that was going to die at its controller's next Beginning Phase anyway can carry a printed 10 into the discount. And the kill is a COST, so 203.3 applies — with no legal friendly unit to kill you simply do not pay it, and Atakhan costs full price rather than becoming unplayable.

synergies.name: The one blink that returns the body to the SAME location, so a "here" play trigger keeps its battlefield

excludes.why: "When you play me FROM FACE DOWN, you may empower something here" — Temporal Breach's replay is a normal play from Banishment, not a play from face down (811.1.c.1 keeps Hide and Play separate), so the trigger never fires.

synergies.why: "Banish a unit, then its owner plays it to the same location, ignoring its cost." Every other re-play route in this file loses the location: a bounce to hand replays under 355.2, which fixes the play location at your base or a battlefield you control, and Portal Rescue names the base outright — which makes every card in this list strictly worse under it, because 359.3.f.2 reads "here" on execution and "here" is then the base. Temporal Breach is the exception written into its own text, so a Sprite Mother or a Royal Guard re-fires at the battlefield it is already standing on. Two mechanics make it safe. 108.6.c makes Banishment the hard-to-recover zone and nothing in the pool returns a card from it, but the replay is part of the same instruction, so the card never rests there. And it says "its owner", so aiming it at an enemy body is a blink for THEM: 191.1 establishes the player who Plays a Game Object as its Controller, so the opponent gets their own play trigger back, which is why this is a friendly-side card. It is [Hidden], so from face down the whole thing costs zero on their turn (811.1.b) — and 811.1.d.2 then confines the target to the battlefield it was hidden at.

synergies.name: 465.2.c.6 prints the whole assignment order — a Tank in front of Caitlyn is what makes her ping forever

excludes.why: "You ignore [Tank] while assigning combat damage here" grants no Tank to anybody — and 767 makes the ignore one-way and scoped to the player the ability names, so it is a key against a wall, not a wall.

synergies.why: Caitlyn prints the Backline EFFECT in prose rather than as a keyword — "I must be assigned combat damage last" — beside "[exhaust]: Deal damage equal to my Might to a unit at a battlefield", so she is a repeatable pinger that only pays if she survives. 465.2.c.6 orders the assignment and its own worked example spells the family out: "That player must assign combat damage first to the unit with Tank, then to the unit with no abilities, then to the unit with Backline." 815.1.c.2 is the hard half — "Units without Tank are invalid assignments until all units with Tank have lethal damage assigned to them" — so an attack whose summed Might is less than the Tank's kills nothing at all, and Caitlyn is not merely last in line but unreachable. Two limits. 465.2.c.8 hands the choice back to the ATTACKER when one body carries two exclusionary requirements, and its worked example is Caitlyn given Tank BY NAME, so the grants in this list (Block, Doran's Shield, Yuumi, Eye of Twilight) must be aimed at another body and never at her. And 815.2 makes a second Tank grant on the same body redundant, so the lever on a printed Tank is its own Might — which is what Kinkou Temple pays for.

synergies.name: 718.2 silences an [Equip] only WHILE attached, so a bounce to hand is the legal way to buy a new carrier
synergies.why: 718.1 — "A card remains in this state until Detached" — is what scopes 718.2, "While in this state, the card's printed Rules Text is Inactive", and 721.2 finishes it: "Inactive Abilities do not trigger, do not apply, and cannot be activated." [Equip] is printed rules text, so an attached Equipment can never pay its own [Equip] again — the printed carve-out on [Weaponmaster], "even if it's already attached", is the proof. 434.1.g closes the obvious workaround: "Attaching a card to its current Top-Most Card will not have any effect." Factory Recall is E1 at [Action] speed and returns the gear to its owner's hand, where the printed text is Active again, so replaying it buys a NEW carrier for one Energy — the only route in the pool that is not an attach EFFECT (Grandmaster at Arms, Forge of the Fluft, Rell, Aphelios' trigger). On a [Quick-Draw] Equipment it is free, because 819.1.d makes the attach a play trigger and no Equip cost is ever determined. Two things the bounce takes with it: 137.3.a stops the Might Bonus "as soon as the card with the Might Bonus is no longer Attached", and 718.3's appended Effect Text goes with it. It answers the opponent's Equipment too — 718.5.b keeps an attached card choosable — which is why an Equipment BURST is not safe behind its carrier.

synergies.name: Bard, Mercurial walks the whole pack onto an open battlefield, so every conquer payoff standing in it is paid

excludes.why: Tryndamere, Barbarian reads "When I conquer AFTER AN ATTACK, if you assigned 5 or more excess damage". Bard's route opens a Showdown under 344.2 with no opposing units, so 465.1 assigns no damage at all and R28 = A makes excess damage attacking Might that was never assigned — the condition is part of the Trigger Condition (383.2.a.1) and can never be met here.
Sivir, Ambitious prints the same "When I conquer after an attack, if you assigned 5 or more excess damage" clause and dies on the same paragraph.
Yeti Brawler needs "3 or more excess damage" assigned. A bloodless conquer assigns none, so the two Gold tokens never arrive.

synergies.why: 383.4.c.2.a is the paragraph: "The Conquer Abilities of Units are put on the Chain as Pending Items after the Unit(s) these effects correspond to are present at a Battlefield when a player gains control of it and gains 1 Victory Point from Conquering." Nothing there asks which unit walked in or which the effect chose — presence is the whole test — and 144.3 makes multiple standard moves ONE action to a shared destination, so a mass relocation scales with how many conquer payoffs are standing in the pack rather than with copies of anything. Bard is the pool's only bulk mover of units of any kind: "move any number of your units to an open battlefield", for the price of exhausting your legend (315.1.b readies it only at your own Awakening, so three copies buy three turns, not three relocations). 170.11.c fixes what the word costs: an open battlefield is one that is "unoccupied and uncontrolled", both conditions, and with no opposing units present 344.2 opens a Showdown at the next Cleanup, 348.2.a establishes Control and 348.2.a.1 says outright "This results in a Conquer". That route has no Attacker designation (807.1.d) and no damage step, which is exactly why the three excess-damage payoffs are excluded and why SFD-116 Yone, Blademaster is one of the BEST partners: his clause reads "a battlefield that was uncontrolled", which an open battlefield is by definition. `stare-down-empties-the-garrison` is the other half of the bloodless-conquer family and shares most of this list: it clears an enemy garrison so ONE battlefield falls. Bard is the opposite operation and the reason 383.4.c.2.a is cited here for the first time — he relocates the payoffs themselves, so the same pack pays again at a SECOND battlefield in the same turn, which is what turns a one-shot conquer into a double-Conquer line (470 and 485.4 cap that at two per turn in a Duel).

synergies.name: Zhonya's Hourglass pays a kill-a-friendly-unit COST and keeps the body

excludes.why: Baited Hook's kill sits AFTER the colon, so it is effect text and not a cost (203.3 never engages), and the payoff then reads "Might up to 1 more than THE KILLED UNIT" — 370.1.a.1 makes the replaced death the same as the kill not occurring, so the referent is gone and the tutor loses its ceiling.

Deathgrip is Riot's own contrast case at 359.3.e.14.b: "Kill a friendly unit. IF YOU DO, give +Might equal to its Might" — a later linked instruction that directly references the replaced game action is not performed, so saving the body costs the whole spell.

synergies.why: 357.2.a reads "Costs that are replaced with other events by replacement effects are still considered paid", and its worked example is this exact pair by name — Cruel Patron paying its additional cost while the player controls the Hourglass, ending "The cost is considered paid, and the player can continue playing Cruel Patron". So every card whose COST kills a friendly unit becomes free of its own price: Cruel Patron, Commander Ledros (one Order Power off per body), Atakhan, Heedless Resurrection, Sacrifice, SFD-178 Blade of the Ruined King's [Equip], VEN-124 Escaped Grayback's [Empower], and OGN-113 Malzahar, Fanatic — whose kill is written BEFORE the colon and is therefore part of the activated ability's cost, not its effect. 370.1.a.1 is the half that must be carried with it or the two read as a contradiction: "A unit's death being replaced by Zhonya's Hourglass is the same as the kill action that caused that death not occurring" — the cost is paid, the death is not, which is why an EFFECT that references the death still fails. The body comes home under 455, so any "While I'm at a battlefield" text is off for a turn, and 808.1.d.1 erases a Deathknell on whatever is saved. The Hourglass is itself [Hidden], so 811.1.b plays it for 0 Energy from the turn after it is hidden. Two of the twelve cards the regex could catch say "friendly GEAR" instead (SFD-084 Jayce, Man of Progress and SFD-160 Zaun Punk) and the predicate leaves them out by construction: the Hourglass saves units only.

synergies.name: One cheap card turns on every [Legion] clause you control at once
synergies.why: 812.2 is the whole rule and it is worth a deck: "All instances of Legion on cards a player controls are satisfied by that player playing a single card." 812.1.b.1 makes each one short for "If you have played another card this turn, this card gains [Text]", and 812.1.c is the trigger this project keeps getting wrong from the other side — the bar is that the other card has been FINALIZED, not that it resolved, so a countered spell still switches the whole Legion board on. Nine other cards carry the keyword and they are Fury and Order, which is one legend pair (OGN-253 Hand of Noxus is itself a Legion card and the free enabler, since its Legion clause rides on an exhaust that costs no card). The cheapest first play is the whole cost of the turn: OGN-012 Noxus Hopeful then costs 2 Energy less, OGN-217 Trifarian Gloryseeker buffs itself, OGN-021 Sun Disc makes the next unit enter ready, OGN-254 Noxian Guillotine kills now instead of on damage, and this anchor's own two Recruit tokens arrive at the battlefield rather than the base. The card that turns them on must be a CARD: 350.2 makes a token played and 185.2.a keeps it from being one, so a token engine satisfies no Legion clause at all.

synergies.name: Last Stand doubles a defender's CURRENT Might, so the [Shield] half is counted and then kept
synergies.why: 432 was cited by nothing in this project until now, and its only worked example is this card. 432.1: "Doubling is the act of increasing a numeric attribute by an amount equal to that attribute’s current value" — the current value, not the printed one — and 432.1.a fixes that amount for the stated duration. The example is worth reading whole: "A unit with 3 base Might and Shield 2 is in combat as a Defender. Since Shield applies, its current Might is 5", Last Stand then gives it +5, "for a current Might of 10. After combat, Shield no longer applies, but the +5 Might from Last Stand does, so the unit’s Might is 8." Two consequences a builder needs: play it AFTER the Defender designation (Last Stand is [Action], so 806.1.b reaches the showdown) and the Shield value is doubled as well as counted; and the increase SURVIVES the designation lapsing, which no other pump in the pool does. 814.1.c is why the timing matters at all ("While I am a defender, I have +X [M]") and 814.2 sums a second granted instance before the doubling reads the total. The rider is real: the body is given [Temporary] and 816.1.b kills it at the start of your own Beginning Phase before scoring, so it can never hold a battlefield the following turn. `eye-of-twilight-tank-on-a-shield-body` uses the same partner list for a different reason — there the Shield raises an unclearable Tank threshold; here it is the number being doubled.

synergies.name: Dune Surfer walks past the opponent's [Tank] wall while yours keeps standing
synergies.why: 767 is the paragraph that makes this a synergy rather than a dispel: "Ignored abilities are only treated as inactive for the specific game action or procedure described, and only by the players directed by the ability." Dune Surfer reads "You ignore [Tank] while assigning combat damage here", so on the same battlefield your own Tank bodies keep every bit of their toll booth against the opponent while their wall stops constraining you — the asymmetry IS the card. What is being switched off is not a small thing: 815.1.b is short for "I must be assigned lethal damage before any other unit with the same controller as me that does not have [Tank]", and 815.1.c.2 makes every non-Tank body an INVALID assignment until each Tank has lethal, so an attack that cannot reach the wall's Might kills nothing at all rather than killing the wrong thing. 465.2.c.6 ("A player must obey all requirements and restrictions on damage assignment if able") is what the ignore removes for you, and because the ability names the game action it is scoped to that assignment and to that battlefield. Note what the ignore does NOT buy: 465.2.c.4 still caps every assignment at the minimum lethal, so walking past a wall changes WHICH bodies die and never how much damage exists — this is not an excess-damage enabler.

synergies.name: A second would-die replacement on Soraka is a fork between two halves of the board, never a doubling

excludes.why: Smite replaces a death with a BANISH, so the body is still removed — it is removal aimed at an enemy, not a second save, and 808.1.d.1's own example is that shape erasing the Deathknell of whatever it catches.

synergies.why: Both halves of this are Riot's worked examples and both name Soraka. 370.4: "A Game Object can apply its Replacement Effects to any qualifying events that occur simultaneously with it leaving the zone that its Replacement Effect is active in" — so a board wipe does not beat her, she still saves the smaller bodies dying beside her. 373.2 is the limit that is not stated anywhere on the cards: "When applying Replacement Effects to events that occur simultaneously, each Replacement Effect may only be applied in one sequence, to any number of events that are qualified to be replaced", and the example is Soraka wearing a Guardian Angel with Recruits dying at her battlefield AND at the base. Saving herself first means her own effect can then only reach one group; letting her die means the garrison goes. So the second replacement buys a CHOICE of which half of the board survives, and a builder who counts it as two saves is counting wrong. Her own clause is scoped twice over, by location ("another unit you control here") and by size ("if it has less Might than me"), and every save in the family relocates: 455 makes a Recall a move to the base without being a Move, which switches off any "While I'm at a battlefield" text for a turn and, with 808.1.d.1, removes the Deathknell of whatever was saved.

synergies.name: Bonus Damage on a SPLIT deal buys a whole extra body, not just an extra point

excludes.why: Ravenborn Tome reads "The next SPELL you play this turn deals 1 Bonus Damage". Volibear's split is a Triggered Ability, not a spell, so the grant never reaches it — the same spell-versus-ability line 417.6.b.3 draws elsewhere.
Consuming Curse's Bonus Damage is self-scoped — "THIS deals 1 Bonus Damage for each card with this name in your trash" — so it augments its own Deal action and grants nothing to anything else.
Dancing Grenade is self-scoped in the same way ("this deals 1 additional Bonus Damage for each time THIS SPELL has dealt damage this turn"), and R15 = A scopes that history to the card itself.

synergies.why: 715.3 is the third shape of Bonus Damage and its worked example is this anchor by name: "If the Deal action Splits damage, then the Bonus Damage applies to the amount of Damage that will be Split. This can alter the number of targets eligible to be chosen." The example attacks with Volibear beside Annie, Fiery and concludes that he "now deals 6 damage split among any number of enemy units at its" battlefield. Against 715.1 (single target) and 715.2 (per target of a multi-target deal), this is the one that changes the SHAPE of the removal: 355.14.c caps the number of targets by the damage available when the spell is played and 355.14.h.1 forbids shrinking the target count below the damage you have to split, so +1 damage against a row of 1-Might bodies is +1 corpse. 714 is the ceiling: "If more than one instance of Bonus Damage is applied or granted to a Deal action, all instances are summed and applied once" — a second source is +1 more, never a doubling. 715.4 keeps Bonus Damage from ever creating a Deal action of its own, and 713 with 417.6.c keeps the whole family disjoint from combat and from excess damage. Two of the six read differently from the other four: OGN-296 Void Gate is worded for the LOCATION ("Spells and abilities deal 1 Bonus Damage to units here"), so it arms the opponent as well and 190.6.d cannot blank it; and SFD-191 Rabadon's Deathcrown is a Signature card tagged Ornn, so 103.2.d.2 makes any list running it an Ornn list.

synergies.name: Commander Ledros pays his Power in token bodies, because a token IS a unit for a cost

excludes.why: Walking Roost gives its Bird to an OPPONENT — 182 lets a creating effect name a different controller — so it never produces a body you may kill as your own additional cost.

synergies.why: His printed cost line — "As you play me, you may kill any number of friendly units as an additional cost", reducing his cost by one Order Power for each body — is the pool's only per-body cost reduction, and the reason it can be paid in tokens is 185.2.d: "Tokens have a type. They follow all rules for their type unless otherwise specified." A token unit is a unit, so 203.3 (a cost whose action is impossible cannot be paid) never engages and 416.1's card-only wording — the trap that kills every recycle-a-token line — is simply not what is being asked for here. The arithmetic is bounded and should be stated: Ledros is 6 Energy and FOUR Order Power, 356.6 floors a cost at 0, so the fifth body onward buys nothing; a four-token turn lands an 8-Might [Deflect] [Ganking] body for 6 Energy. Nothing comes back — 186.1 makes a token cease to exist the instant it enters any non-board zone, so it never reaches the trash and no reanimation or recycle can see it, which is also why this is a strictly better fodder than killing real cards. And the bodies must already be on the board when he is played: the additional cost is paid during the steps of playing him (357), not afterwards.

synergies.name: A [Temporary] garrison hands a conquer battlefield back every turn, so its trigger fires more than once a game

excludes.why: Petricite Monument is GEAR. 323.6 strips Control only from a player with no UNITS occupying the battlefield, and 323.7 recalls unattached gear at every Cleanup anyway, so a Temporary gear is never the garrison that has to die.
Sumpworks Map is gear, for the same reason.
Spinning Axe is an Equipment; its [Temporary] kills the gear, never the carrier, so the battlefield is not handed back.
Turn to Dust gives a GEAR [Temporary] — it can never condemn the body holding the battlefield.

LeBlanc, Everywhere at Once reads "Your [Temporary] effects at my battlefield don't trigger" and R10 = A rules that this does switch the kill off (816.1 makes [Temporary] a Triggered Ability keyword), which is the exact opposite of what the cycle needs.
Petal Pixie only READS your [Temporary] bodies for its own Might; it grants the keyword to nothing.

synergies.why: Fourteen of the 66 battlefields carry a when-you-conquer-here trigger, and most of them fire once a game, because 315.2.b.2 makes the Hold mandatory, 470 caps Scoring at once per battlefield per turn and 348.2.a refuses Control to a player who already has it. The fix is to stop controlling it on purpose: 816.1.b makes [Temporary] short for "At the start of this permanent's controller's Beginning Phase, before scoring, kill this.", 319.6 then 323.6 ("Players lose control of any controlled Battlefields without their Units occupying them if the turn is in an Open State and there is no Showdown or Combat ongoing there") strip Control in the same Cleanup, and the battlefield is open again for a Main-Phase walk-in. It costs nothing in exposure, because 144.1.a-c with 312.2.a leave the opponent no state in which they both hold priority and may move a body in. What it buys is the TRIGGER and never a second point — 470 is untouched. Treasure Hoard is the cheapest payoff to cycle (1 Energy for a Gold gear token, exhausted, so 187.5's own exhaust makes it Power only from your next Awakening unless SFD-171 Renata Glasc, Industrialist is out, R25 = A). The disposable body must be a UNIT and it must be the ONLY one there, which is why the six excludes below are excludes and not partners.

synergies.name: The Baron Pit is the one destination a unit may Standard-Move to from anywhere, so a move payoff lands at a battlefield every turn instead of every other turn

excludes.why: Corrupt Enforcer's move clause is the DRAWBACK half of the card — "When I move to a battlefield, discard 1" — while its payoff is "When I win a combat, draw 1". Firing the move half every turn instead of every other turn is a cost, not a gain; this is the doubled-drawback false positive.

synergies.why: 187.9 defines the token in the rules themselves: "The Baron Pit battlefield token is a domainless battlefield token with “Units can move here from anywhere.”" Every movement fact this project owns is keyword-shaped — [Ganking] per unit, [Accelerate] per body, an effect move per card — and 187.9 is the one DESTINATION-shaped exception. 144.4 restricts where a Standard Move may go and 144.4.c.1 gives battlefield-to-battlefield only to [Ganking], so a body without the keyword pendulums battlefield, base, battlefield, and half of its legs end at the base where a "when I move to a battlefield" payoff does not fire. With the Pit on the board every leg can end at a battlefield. It does not add moves — 144.2 makes exhausting the unit the cost of the Standard Move, 420.3.a repeats it, and 415.3.a readies the body only in your own Awakening — it makes each move reach twice as far. Nothing removes the Pit once it is there: 170.3 "Battlefields cannot be Killed during the course of regular play", 170.4 "Battlefields cannot be Moved", and 185.2.e ends "Token battlefields and legends can’t be recycled." Two prices are printed on the card and belong in any deckbuilding decision. Baron Nashor is mono-Chaos at 10 Energy plus 3 Power, so the legend must carry Chaos and the Pit arrives late; and the token's clause says "Units", not "you", so 190.6.d cannot blank it and it serves the opponent's bodies exactly as well as yours. The scoring half of the same token is a separate fact: 483.4 defines Battlefield Count as what is "contributed by players", 485.4 sets that at 2 for a Duel, and a battlefield a CARD adds is outside the count — so the per-turn Score ceiling becomes 3 under 470, with 471.1.b.1 then taxing a Conquer-based eighth point ("If the player has Scored every Battlefield this turn") while 471.1.a.1 leaves a Hold-based one alone.

synergies.name: Eye of the Herald makes a Recruit wherever its carrier lands, so every effect move is a second token and it is born at a battlefield

partner.textMatches: [Mm]ove (a|an|another|up to \w+|any number of|all) (friendly units?|units? you control|different units? you control)

synergies.why: Eye of the Herald prints its payoff in the [Effect] half — "When I move, play a 1 :rb_might: Recruit unit token here" — and 434.1.c ("The Top-Most card has all Effect Text of all cards Attached to it appended to its Rules Text"), 718.3 and 719.1 append that text to the CARRIER, where 053.1 ("Units and legends say “I,” “me,” etc.") makes "I" the unit and not the gear; 053.2 and 136.2.d reserve "this" for the attached card. So the trigger watches the carrier's movement. Two things follow. First, a Standard Move already fires it once a turn for free — 144.2 makes exhausting the unit the whole cost, and 420.3.a puts that cost on the Standard Move alone — so every card in this list is a SECOND Recruit in the same turn, and 449 with 420.2.b make an effect move a Move for this purpose (R9 = A). Second, 359.3.f.2 checks information referenced in an instruction "on execution of the instruction", so "here" is read where the carrier has arrived: a mover that ends at a battlefield mints the body AT that battlefield, which is the standing token bottleneck of this project (49 token-makers, 18 of them printed "at your base") answered by a 1-Energy Order gear. FIVE of the fourteen move only to BASE, and they are named because a reader who does not check will assume the position comes with the token: SFD-043 Emperor's Divide, OGS-011 Flash, OGN-184 The Syren, VEN-139 Rogue Assassin and OGN-285 Reaver's Row, which is banned in both formats. Each still mints the Recruit, but at the base, which is where a Standard Move would have put it anyway; they are partners for the extra body and not for the position, and they are kept rather than excluded because the token is real. At the other end, OGN-173 Ride the Wind readies the unit it moved, which hands the Standard Move back (144.2, 415.1) and makes one card TWO Recruits in the same turn.

synergies.name: An "attack or defend" clause is BOTH triggers, and Iascylla is the free repeating way to fire the defend half on your own turn

excludes.why: Wielder of Water pays only "while I'm attacking or defending ALONE", and 740.2.a reads alone as an own-side measurement — "A unit is alone when there are no other friendly units at the same location." The enemy body is dragged to Iascylla's own battlefield and Iascylla is standing there, so the condition can never be met on the event this rule schedules.
Mask of Foresight pays "when a friendly unit attacks or defends alone", the same 740.2.a measurement, and fails for the same reason: Iascylla is a second friendly body at that location.

Fiora, Peerless needs "one on one", which 740.2.b defines as BOTH units being alone — so it needs your side down to one as well. Iascylla standing at the battlefield breaks it from your side before the opponent's garrison is even counted.

synergies.why: 383.4.e and 383.4.f are the same sentence twice: "Attack Triggers are Triggered Abilities that trigger when a Unit or Player gains the Attacker designation for the first time during a combat", and the Defender mirror. A clause worded "when I attack or defend" therefore satisfies both and is two triggers on one card — the shape the rules state outright for the other pair at 823.1.b, where Hunt is both a Conquer and a Hold effect. The attack half is yours to schedule; the defend half is the OPPONENT'S, and a player who has read the card simply stops attacking that battlefield. Iascylla schedules it for free: "When I hold, at the start of your next Main Phase, you may move an enemy unit to this battlefield." 450 makes the destination Contested because it is "an Uncontested Battlefield not controlled by the controller of the Unit or Units that moved" and 190.3.a.1 says the same from the other side, so 464.2.c.1 — "The Attacker is the player whose unit(s) applied the Contested status to the Battlefield" — makes THEM the attacker on YOUR turn, 323.9 stages the Combat at the next Cleanup and 323.13 opens it. 464.2.e.1 puts the Defender's triggered abilities on the Chain last, which 340.1 resolves FIRST. The engine costs nothing beyond Iascylla: her trigger has no cost, 315.2.b.2 Holds every battlefield you control every turn, and 392 executes the delayed half "regardless of whether the source of the Delayed Ability is still on the board". One partner is paid by the drag itself rather than merely by it: UNL-143 Kha'Zix, Mutating Horror asks that "an enemy unit is alone here", and 740.2.a measures alone on the unit's own side, so the single body Iascylla moves in is alone there by construction. Two limits. 383.4.e.2.a and 383.4.f.2.a check the condition once per combat, so nothing here fires twice in one combat. And the payoff has to be standing at Iascylla's battlefield, which is why the three "alone" and "one on one" cards below are excludes and not partners. SFD-020 Draven, Vanquisher is in the match list and is banned in both formats; the matcher drops it from any list it reads, and it is left in the rule rather than excluded because a ban is a legality fact and not a defect in the pairing.

synergies.name: Quick-Draw never DETERMINES an Equip cost, so Jax attaches every Equipment in the deck for free and at Reaction speed

excludes.why: Long Sword already prints [Quick-Draw], and 819.2 is explicit: "Multiple instances of Quick-Draw do not trigger separately and have no effect beyond the first." Jax's grant is worth nothing on it — the second-trigger-is-a-no-op false positive.
Sterak's Gage already prints [Quick-Draw]; 819.2 makes the grant a no-op.
Cloth Armor already prints [Quick-Draw]; 819.2 makes the grant a no-op.
Spinning Axe already prints [Quick-Draw]; 819.2 makes the grant a no-op.

synergies.why: 819.1.d is the whole rule: "Quick-Draw is functionally short for “[Reaction]” and “When you play this, attach it to a Unit you control.”" Both halves matter and this catalogue has been treating them as one thing. 818.1 makes Equip "an Activated Ability keyword" with a cost, and 818.1.c.3 allows that cost to include "both resource costs and non-resource costs"; a Quick-Draw attach is a PLAY trigger, so no Equip cost is ever determined at all. That is strictly stronger than [Weaponmaster], which 821.1.c only DISCOUNTS by one rainbow and which 821.1.c.6 says outright does not activate the Equip. The difference is invisible until an Equip cost has a non-resource half, and three Equipment in the pool have one — SFD-150 Last Rites ("Recycle 2 cards from your trash"), SFD-178 Blade of the Ruined King ("Kill a friendly unit") and UNL-158 Shepherd's Heirloom ("Spend 1 XP") — where a rainbow rebate buys nothing and Jax deletes the cost entirely. The [Reaction] half (813.1.c.1: "This can be played during Closed States on any player's turn") turns every Equipment in the list into a combat trick that lands after the attackers are designated. Jax's grant reads "everywhere", so it reaches an Equipment played from anywhere it can be played from, not only from hand. Two prices are honest to state: the Equipment's own PLAY cost is untouched — Quick-Draw removes the attach, never the card — and 434.1.g makes attaching to the current Top-Most Card do nothing, so the free attach is one new carrier per Equipment played, not a shuttle.

synergies.name: The Power Nexus is paid at FINALIZATION, where nobody has priority, and 444.2.c is the only thing that can produce Power there

excludes.why: Daughter of the Void's Add reads "Use only to play spells". The Power Nexus's point is a Triggered Ability of a battlefield, not a spell, so this rainbow can never pay it.
Fire Below the Mountain's Add reads "Use only to play gear or use gear abilities". The Nexus is a battlefield's Triggered Ability and is neither.

synergies.why: "When you hold here, you may pay four rainbow to score 1 point" is a cost written at the start of a Triggered Ability's effect, so 204.3.a makes it the ability's BASE COST and 383.3.b.1 says "The cost must be paid in order to finalize the Triggered Ability to the Chain." That window is brutal: 312.2.c — "When the turn is in a Closed State, all pending chain items finish being finalized" — hands out no priority in between, so nothing can be played or activated there by the ordinary route, and 381 bars every Activated Ability outside your own Open State anyway. 444.2.c is the one door and it was cited by nothing in this project until 2026-09-12: "Players may activate abilities that Add resources with the Reaction keyword at any time that they are instructed to Pay resources. Those abilities finalize and resolve immediately, ignoring normal restrictions." The instruction to pay IS the window. That is why the Nexus needs no Mind card and runs in any identity at all — 164.2 gives every Basic Rune two abilities and BOTH carry [Reaction] (164.2.a "[E]: [Reaction] — Add [1].", 164.2.b "Recycle this: [Reaction] — Add [C]."), and 135.2.e.5.a lets any domain pay a rainbow cost: "When required as a cost, [A] can be paid by Power of any Domain." What this list adds is Power that costs no rune: each of these is a 0-Energy source that is READY at the Hold, because 315.1.b readies everything you control in the Awaken Phase and 315.2.b.2's Scoring Step comes after it, and 813.1.c.2 lifts 381 for them. Two things to know before building on it. The decision is blind — 383.3.e.2.a puts the choice to perform the trigger "during finalization", 383.3.e.2.b removes it from the chain if you decline, and 312.2.c means no response has happened yet. And four of the matches are Gold-token makers whose [Reaction] Add is printed inside the TOKEN's reminder text (UNL-018 Yeti Brawler, UNL-073 Deadly Flourish, UNL-145 Pyke Returned, UNL-185 Bloodharbor Ripper); they are genuine and they are slow, because 187.5 costs the Gold its own exhaust and every Gold in the pool is played exhausted, so 415.3.a makes it live only from your next Awakening — a Gold banked from an earlier turn pays a quarter of the Nexus, a Gold minted this turn pays nothing.

synergies.name: Sun Disc lets a unit use its exhaust ability the turn it lands, and "enters ready" is still not a ready

excludes.why: Fretful Feline pays "When I become ready", and that is exactly what an enters-ready grant does not do. 415.1: "Readying is an action that marks a non-spell Game Object on the board as available for action" — a unit that ENTERS ready was never on the board to be marked. 805.6 states the mechanism for the keyword form ("It does not enter exhausted and then become ready") and 805.6.a states the consequence ("Accelerate will not interact with, or trigger, abilities that are affected by units becoming ready"); the Sun Disc grants the same replacement with no keyword on it, so the same closure applies.
Jayce, Hammer in Hand pays "When I become ready" and fails for the identical reason, 415.1 with 805.6 / 805.6.a.

Arena Kingpin prints "I enter ready" unconditionally, so the Sun Disc's grant is applied to an event that is already replaced; 370.2 allows a Replacement Effect to apply only once to an event, and there is nothing left for the second one to do.

Yeti Brawler matches only on the reminder text of the Gold gear TOKEN he plays ("[Reaction][>] Kill this, exhaust: [Add] rainbow"). That exhaust belongs to the token, not to Yeti Brawler, and the Sun Disc grant is on the UNIT you play — the nested-quote false positive.
Pyke, Returned matches on the same nested Gold-token reminder text; his own abilities carry no exhaust cost, so entering ready buys him nothing.

synergies.why: 143.4 — "Units enter the Board exhausted" — is what makes an exhaust-cost ability on a freshly played unit dead for a turn, because 415.3.a hands the exhaust back only "during the Awakening Phase on their turn". The Sun Disc buys that turn back for 2 Energy and 1 Power: "exhaust: [Legion] — The next unit you play this turn enters ready", where 812.1 makes [Legion] a Dependent Keyword and 812.1.c switches it on: "As long as a card different than the one with the Legion ability has been Finalized by you on the same turn then the Dependent Ability is Active on the card with Legion.". Every partner here is a unit whose text prints a cost containing its own exhaust, so the grant is worth a whole activation on the turn it lands. The rule exists as much for its excludes as for its list. An enters-ready grant is NOT a ready: 415.1 defines Readying as marking a Game Object already on the board, and 805.6 / 805.6.a say both halves of that for [Accelerate] in the rules' own words. The pool prints exactly THREE become-ready payoffs and all three are mono-Body — VEN-071 Fretful Feline and VEN-088 Jayce, Hammer in Hand, both excluded below, and OGN-143 Pirate's Haven, which is a BATTLEFIELD and therefore outside this rule's partner types, named here so the trap is recorded in the one place a reader will meet it. The Sun Disc is mono-Fury, so a Fury/Body legend can hold the Disc and all three of them, and a line built on that pairing is refuted on its face.

synergies.name: The Academy grants a [Repeat] the spell never printed, and 820.2.a lets the second execution pick the other mode

excludes.why: Blind Fury is not modal. Its "Choose one" names one of the cards each opponent just revealed, not one of several printed modes, so 820.2.a - the paragraph this rule stands on - has nothing to apply to. It is still a legal target for the grant and a Repeat would execute the whole spell twice; it is excluded because the reason this rule gives would be the wrong reason.

synergies.why: "When you hold here, give your next spell this turn [Repeat] equal to its base cost" is the only card in the pool that hands [Repeat] to a spell that prints none — SFD-211 Marai Spire only DISCOUNTS a printed one and UNL-146 Syndra, Transcendent grants hers only inside a showdown. 820.1.b defines the keyword ("Repeat is an optional cost that a player may pay to execute the effect of their spells and abilities a second time") and 820.2.a is why a MODAL spell is the best thing to spend it on: "Choices made for the additional execution do not have to be the same as the choices made for the initial execution." Riot's worked example for that paragraph is Rocket Barrage, a modal spell in this pool, by name. So one card buys both modes. 135.2.b.3 is the limit and it is the reason a granted Repeat is not simply two spells: "If the card is given Repeat and the Repeat cost is paid, this instruction will not execute because the Repeat execution does not happen until resolution" — an instruction that self-describes as happening AS YOU PLAY is performed once, and 820.1.d.2 ignores anything not performed on resolution. Two of the twelve rows already print [Repeat] of their own, SFD-077 Rocket Barrage and UNL-182 Curtain Call; they are not false positives but the best rows in the list, because 820.1.c.2 makes each instance payable individually, so the Academy's grant is a THIRD execution there rather than a second. The price is printed on the battlefield: the Repeat cost EQUALS the spell's base cost, so the cheap modal spells are the point (VEN-052 Mesmerize at 1 Energy plus 1 Power is the cheapest in the list) and an expensive one doubles its own bill. And a battlefield is not a tutor: 103.4.c forbids a second copy of a battlefield name, 485.4.a has each player provide three and 485.5 "randomly selects" one, so the Academy is on the board one game in three.

synergies.name: Highlander is the Reaction form of Zhonya's trick: the kill-a-friendly-unit cost is paid and the body comes back

excludes.why: Baited Hook's kill sits AFTER the colon, so it is effect text and not a cost — 203.3 never engages — and the payoff then reads "Might up to 1 more than the killed unit". 370.1.a.1 makes the replaced death "the same as the kill action that caused that death not occurring", so the referent is gone and the tutor loses its ceiling.

Deathgrip is Riot's own contrast case at 359.3.e.14.b: "Kill a friendly unit. If you do, …" is a later linked instruction that directly references the replaced game action, so saving the body costs the whole spell.

synergies.why: 357.2.a is the rule and its worked example is this exact interaction with the other card: "Costs that are replaced with other events by replacement effects are still considered paid", worked through Cruel Patron paying its kill-a-friendly-unit cost into a Zhonya's Hourglass. Highlander does the same job from hand — "[Reaction] Choose a friendly unit. The next time it would die this turn, heal it, exhaust it, and recall it instead" — and the difference from OGN-077 Zhonya's Hourglass is worth a deck slot in both directions. The Hourglass is a permanent that must be on the board or hidden BEFORE the turn, and it kills itself to work, so it is one use and it is visible; Highlander is 4 Energy and no Power, sits in hand, is aimed after the cost has been announced (813.1.c.1 admits it in any Closed State on any player's turn), and costs no board presence. What it costs instead is position and the Deathknell: 455 defines a Recall as relocation "from anywhere to its Base without it being a Move", so anything the body was doing at a battlefield stops until it walks back, and 808.1.d.1 removes that body's own Deathknell from the chain because it never reaches the Trash. One trap belongs beside every use of this family and it is not about the partner at all: 390.5.a gives the delayed shield a window only "as long as that Game Object is in an appropriate zone", and 359.3.e.4 says a game object that leaves and returns "is no longer a legal target, because it's not treated as the same object" — so returning your own shielded unit to hand CLOSES the shield you already paid for, and replaying it does not restore it. The other three members of the family are OGN-023 Unlicensed Armory, UNL-175 Tactical Retreat and SFD-194 Counter Strike, and the last one is different in kind: it PREVENTS the damage instead, so it moves nothing and is the only one of the four that keeps a "while I'm at a battlefield" static switched on.

synergies.name: A Prevent Value is counted when damage is ASSIGNED, so Ki Barrier on a [Tank] makes the whole garrison unassignable for seven more

excludes.why: Dune Surfer reads "You ignore [Tank] while assigning combat damage here" — it is the pool's answer to a Tank wall, not a member of one. 766 makes an ignored ability "treated as inactive for the purposes of the game action or procedure", so a Dune Surfer on your own board switches off the mandatory-assignment rule this whole rule stands on.

synergies.why: The naive reading of a Prevent is that it absorbs damage after the fact. 437.5.a says it is counted before any is dealt: "Damage can be assigned to a Unit up to a value that would be Lethal considering the Prevent Value of all Prevent Actions on a Unit, following the normal rules for damage assignment", and Riot's example is a 2 Might unit with a 3-point Prevent needing 5 assigned. Put that on a [Tank] and 815.1.c.2 does the rest: "Units without Tank are invalid assignments until all units with Tank have lethal damage assigned to them." So Ki Barrier's seven is not seven damage saved on one body, it is seven more the attacker must find before a single point may legally be assigned to anything else you control, and 465.2.c.4 forbids them from banking the surplus elsewhere. 437.3 is what makes it hold up across a turn rather than one hit — "reduce the Prevent Value being tracked on the Unit affected by the Prevent action by the prevented amount" — a pool spent down, so several small pings eat it one at a time instead of one ping wasting it. Ki Barrier is Order, 2 Energy and 1 Power, [Reaction], and it cantrips, so it is bought after the attackers are designated (464.2.c.3) and before 465.2.c assigns. Two limits. 465.2.c.10 marks the far end of the scale — "If a unit cannot be dealt damage, then no amount of damage can be considered lethal. Such a unit is exempt from any considerations of mandatory assignment" — so a FULL immunity would take the body out of the assignment order entirely and switch the wall off; a finite Prevent Value is what keeps it a legal, expensive assignment. And this rule is about the ASSIGNMENT order only: 437.5 keeps the damage assignable in the first place, and nothing here protects the body from a kill by effect, which reads Might and not damage.
